title: Joints and body movements
note: Joints are classed by structure (fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial) and by how much they move (synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, diarthrosis). All synovial joints are diarthroses. Movement terms come in opposite pairs, such as flexion and extension or abduction and adduction.

read.title: Structure decides movement
text: Joints can be sorted two ways, and the two systems line up closely. The structural system asks what holds the bones together. In fibrous joints, such as the sutures of the skull, dense connective tissue binds the bones tightly. In cartilaginous joints, such as the pubic symphysis and the discs between vertebrae, cartilage unites them. In synovial joints, the bones are not directly joined at all: they meet inside a fluid-filled cavity enclosed by a capsule.

The functional system asks how much the joint moves. Immovable joints are synarthroses, slightly movable joints are amphiarthroses, and freely movable joints are diarthroses. Sutures are synarthroses that protect the brain. The pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis that adds stability to the pelvis. Every synovial joint is a diarthrosis.

Synovial joints share a set of parts. Hyaline articular cartilage caps the bone ends, a synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes lubricating fluid, and ligaments limit excess motion. The shapes of the bone ends then set the range of motion. A hinge such as the elbow bends in one plane, a condyloid knuckle moves in two, and a ball-and-socket joint such as the hip moves in all three and can rotate.

q.q: What makes a synovial joint different from the other structural types?
o: The bones meet in a fluid-filled cavity
